name: PicoClaw
vibe_summary: An ultra-lightweight Go rewrite of the OpenClaw-style personal AI assistant, built by Sipeed to run on $10 boards with under 10MB of RAM. It trades OpenClaw's feature breadth for extreme portability across x86, ARM, RISC-V, MIPS, and LoongArch.
best_for: Running an AI assistant on cheap SBCs and embedded boards
Users who want minimal RAM/CPU footprint
Self-hosters targeting non-x86 architectures like RISC-V
avoid_if: You need OpenClaw's full plugin and channel ecosystem
You want a mature multi-user or team deployment
You need battle-tested sandboxing for untrusted tool execution
openclaw_advantages: Runs on $10 hardware with under 10MB RAM
Near-instant boot time versus OpenClaw's heavier runtime
Single Go binary deployable across many CPU architectures
Far lower infrastructure cost for always-on assistants
openclaw_disadvantages: Less mature sandboxing and security hardening
Fewer messaging channels and UI features
Younger project with a smaller contributor base
confidence_summary: Strong evidence from the README, active recent commits, and a recent v0.3.1 release confirm an actively maintained, genuinely lightweight OpenClaw alternative. Security posture and ecosystem maturity are inferred from limited sources, so those ratings carry moderate uncertainty.

overview_markdown:
PicoClaw is an independent open-source AI assistant written entirely in Go by Sipeed, inspired by NanoBot and positioned as an ultra-lightweight alternative to OpenClaw. Its headline claim is running a full agent loop on $10 hardware with under 10MB of RAM and millisecond boot times — roughly 99% less memory than OpenClaw — with builds for x86_64, ARM64, MIPS, RISC-V, and LoongArch. Notably, the project describes a 'self-bootstrapping' development process where the AI agent itself drove the architecture migration and code optimization.

Architecturally, PicoClaw is a single Go binary with a provider abstraction layer supporting Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible, and Bedrock-style APIs, plus a tool registry with per-agent allowlists and enable flags. Recent commits show active hardening: configurable model fallback chains, fixes to Anthropic tool_use serialization for reloaded history, and safer write_file behavior that steers agents toward non-destructive edit tools. A v0.3.1 release shipped in July 2026, and the project maintains docs in ten languages with active Discord and WeChat communities.

Compared to OpenClaw, PicoClaw deliberately sacrifices ecosystem breadth — fewer channels, plugins, and UI surfaces — in exchange for extreme portability and cost efficiency. It is best understood as the edge/embedded branch of the OpenClaw design space: ideal for always-on assistants on SBCs, routers, and low-power boards, but not yet a replacement for OpenClaw's mature multi-channel, multi-user deployments.
